The Guardian picture essay Troubled waters: life during wartime for Iranians on the strait of Hormuz One of the ships stranded in the Strait of Hormuz. Despite US-Israeli airstrikes and Tehran’s attacks on shipping, the waterway still has to provide a lifeline for those that live and work there By Stefanie Glinski ; photographs by Mohammad Mohsenifar in Bandar Abbas/on Hormuz Island Wed 21 Oct 2026 06.00 BST Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 06.01 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Capt Farouq turns the wheel as he watches the ferry terminal of Bandar Abbas grow smaller, its bright lights flickering in the distance. In front of him, the navigation radar beeps periodically, its green and pink lights glowing in the darkness. The ferry, today at about half capacity with roughly 100 passengers, turns and heads into the darkness of the strait of Hormuz. View image in fullscreen 
 
 Capt Farouq pulls into the deeper waters 
 
 View image in fullscreen 
 
 He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home 
 
 Farouq, 39, sits comfortably in his cabin, overlooking the pitch black horizon as he sails towards Hormuz Island, a short commute of about half an hour from the Iranian mainland’s Haqqani Port, for 340,000 toman, about £1. He is relaxed and smiles as he pulls into the deeper waters. He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home. Farouq says the crossings have not stopped since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February, although passenger numbers are down and the journey has become more dangerous. For months, Farouq has heard explosions coming from the strait, unclear as to whether that is air defence or attacks, or both. Tonight is no different. Inside the ferry, passengers say they have gotten used to the sounds too, and, to an extent, the war itself. They drink tea and smoke cigarettes. Some nap, while others entertain their children. It’s hot and humid, the air thick, the windows fogged with condensation. View image in fullscreen 
 
 One of the ships stranded in the strait of Hormuz 
 
 Even with a fragile ceasefire in place, here on the coast, it has barely felt as though the war has stopped. According to Iranian government sources, attacks on the southern port of Bandar Abbas have damaged 760 fishing and commercial vessels. Farouq says his own ferry was also damaged by shrapnel while docked at the port, though it was quickly repaired. Since the start of the war, Iranian forces have repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to cross the strait. In the first week of October alone, at least 12 attacks were reported against oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers, sending oil prices back above $100 a barrel . With pressure mounting on the US president, Donald Trump, before the midterm elections, he is rumoured to be once again considering strikes. But beyond the headlines and global markets, the strait is first and foremost a lifeline for many Iranians living in the southern province of Hormozgan. View image in fullscreen 
 
 Fishers returning from sea 
 
 View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen 
 
 Fishers in Bandar Abbas selling their catch on the street 
 
 Fishers, captains and harbour workers all depend on the strait for their livelihoods and the war has made their work increasingly difficult. Fishers can no longer venture as far out, ports have come under attack, and many people fled Bandar Abbas in the early months of the war for smaller, more remote villages in search of safety. View image in fullscreen 
 
 Local residents fishing for their own daily consumption 
 
 View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Anvar Sadat, a 38-year-old fisher who works at Bandar Abbas’s fish market, says business has slowed and that making ends meet has become increasingly difficult. “Fishing boats can’t go out as freely as before the war, and our movement is restricted,” he says, adding that several of his colleagues in the city have been killed in attacks. View image in fullscreen 
 
 Anvar Sadat, who works at the fish market in Bandar Abbas 
 
 “This place was hell,” says Abdul Salam, a 45-year-old garbage collector. The beaches, particularly those near the port, were among the most dangerous places during the height of the war, he says, describing heavy attacks that forced him to stop working almost entirely to avoid the risk. Life on the island, however, has been different, Farouq explains as he steers into the small, dimly lit port of Hormuz Island, his last crossing of the day before heading back to his family for the night.
